source.title: SDAR: A Synergistic Diffusion-AutoRegression Paradigm for Scalable Sequence Generation
source.authors: Shuang Cheng; Yihan Bian; Da-Wei Liu; Yu-Hua Jiang; Yi-Hao Liu; Lin-Feng Zhang; Qian Yao; Zhong-Bo Tian; Wen-Hai Wang; Qi-Peng Guo; Kai Chen; Biqing Qi; Bo-Wen Zhou

record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps downstream benchmark performance across SDAR model sizes, a different measure from the held-out pretraining loss in the claim. It therefore tests V6's scale-to-downstream-performance part, but not the stated pretraining-loss laws or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream scores across SDAR scales, which bear on V6. It does not report held-out pretraining-loss scaling curves, small-run fits predicting much larger runs, or fixed-compute loss-minimising parameter/token allocations. Its separate inference-throughput results are not loss-scaling results. Comparisons of AR and SDAR performance and results cited from prior work are not included as rows here.
record.test_reason: Its own Table 2 reports downstream benchmark scores for SDAR-Chat models at 1.7B, 4B, 8B and 30B-A3B. That bears on V6 (downstream scores improving with scale) in a new setting: AR models converted to blockwise diffusion. It is not T2, because no new method targets the scaling question. The sizes come from different Qwen3 base checkpoints, and the largest is MoE with 3B active parameters. No curve is fitted and no loss is measured, so only the 'improves with scale' part of V6 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say SDAR 'scales without compromise': performance improves with size (MMLU 62.9 to 82.8), and they state gains are consistent across all benchmark categories, which overstates their own Table 2. They also conclude that larger models tolerate bigger blocks and looser thresholds, giving higher parallel speedup. They do not test loss-based scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study converts autoregressive models to blockwise diffusion and evaluates downstream capabilities and inference efficiency; it does not fit the original held-out-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal parameter/token split.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream scores vary by benchmark and model size; several benchmark series are nonmonotonic. The main size sweep uses block length 4 and static greedy decoding.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger SDAR models tolerate larger block sizes and lower confidence thresholds with less performance loss, and achieve higher tokens per forward pass (Figs 3-6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness to parallel decoding and decoding efficiency of block-diffusion LMs increase with model scale.

fits_no_version.finding: In a controlled 2B, 1T-token comparison, the AR model reaches lower training loss and better downstream scores than a masked diffusion model (Section 4, Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At equal compute, the AR objective is more compute-efficient than the masked-diffusion objective.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The V6 evidence consists of benchmark scores at four SDAR scales, without uncertainty estimates or a fitted predictive relationship. Some benchmark scores are nonmonotonic; the 30B-A3B model is MoE, while the smaller listed models are not stated to be MoE in this scale table.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 also reports TriviaQA, MMMLU-lite, and CMMLU across the same four sizes (12 rows). Omitted to stay within the 60-row cap after retaining 15 other benchmark series; the retained rows include the stated MMLU example and the nonmonotonic or flat series.

untested.parts: Predictability: no fitted scale law or forecast. Improvement with pretraining loss: no loss reported. Controlled scale sweep: the sizes are different Qwen3 bases, and the top model is MoE.
No held-out pretraining-loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits extrapolated to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation of parameters versus tokens.
No depth or width comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits in other modalities or regimes. The block-diffusion adaptation is not fitted to any law.
No fitted exponents or fitting-choice comparisons.

missing.what: AR-Chat counterparts (same CPT+SFT pipeline) across 1.7B/4B/8B/30B-A3B. Some series are non-monotone too, e.g. IFEval 43.3, 58.4, 60.8, 57.7 and AIME-24 7.1, 12.9, 10.0, 15.4. A researcher would need these to tell whether the dips are SDAR-specific.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's ARC-C rows r01-r03 are shifted: r01 took the AR-1.7B column value. The scale sweep is not controlled. Each size is a different Qwen3 base given 50B tokens of CPT plus SFT, and 30B-A3B is MoE, so the dips at the top step may reflect active-parameter count. No uncertainty is reported, so small differences (e.g. GSM8K 91.3 vs 91.4, IFEval 61.4 vs 60.6) are within likely noise. Calling this a 'scaling law' analysis is loose: no curves are fitted.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining-loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run power-law fits or tests of predictions on much larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or fitted parameter/token allocation trend.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No test of the claimed power-law form in other modalities or the listed training regimes.
Tests downstream benchmark scores across model sizes; does not test predictability from pretraining loss or forecast scores using a fitted scale law.
Does not test fitted exponents, loss-curve bending, or dependence of compute-optimal allocation on setup or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: SDAR-Chat 1.7B to 30B-A3B, block length 4, static greedy decoding; ARC-C, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, MathBench, AIME-25, HumanEval, HumanEval-X, LCB-v6
relationships.reason: Scores rise at each size step: e.g. MMLU 62.9 to 82.8, HumanEval 61.6 to 87.2, LCB-v6 5.7 to 21.7 (r01-r12, r21-r24, r29-r32, r37-r40, r45-r48, r53-r60). This shows monotone gains only; no fitted predictable law.
relationships.display_finding: Scores increased at every size step, including MMLU from 62.9 to 82.8, HumanEval from 61.6 to 87.2, and LCB-v6 from 5.7 to 21.7, without a fitted predictive law.

relationships.condition: Same sweep; GPQA-diamond, IFEval, Math500, MBPP, AIME-24, LMB-Hard
relationships.reason: 30B-A3B (MoE, ~3B active) scores below 8B on GPQA (36.7 vs 40.2), IFEval, Math500 and MBPP. AIME-24 is flat at 10.0 from 1.7B to 8B. LMB-Hard barely moves from 1.7B to 4B (r13-r20, r25-r28, r33-r36, r41-r44, r49-r52).
relationships.display_finding: 30B-A3B trailed 8B on GPQA, 36.7 versus 40.2, and on IFEval, Math500 and MBPP; AIME-24 stayed at 10.0 from 1.7B to 8B, while LMB-Hard barely changed from 1.7B to 4B.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SDAR-Chat size sweep on ARC-C, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, MathBench, AIME-25, LMB-Hard, HumanEval, HumanEval-X, and LCB-v6
reader_labels.reason: Scores rise across the reported 1.7B, 4B, 8B, and 30B-A3B series (r01-r12, r21-r24, r29-r32, r37-r44, r45-r48, r53-r60). This supports improvement with scale in these tested settings, not a fitted law or forecast.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: SDAR-Chat size sweep on GPQA-diamond, IFEval, Math500, MBPP, and AIME-24
reader_labels.reason: Several benchmarks are nonmonotonic or flat across some scale steps: the 30B-A3B score is below 8B on GPQA-diamond, IFEval, Math500, and MBPP, while AIME-24 is unchanged at 4B and 8B before rising at 30B-A3B (r13-r20, r25-r28, r33-r36, r49-r52).
